label: "Bourne Again" re-implementation
citation: Ramey, C. & Fox, B. (current ed.). Bash Reference Manual, §1.1 "What is Bash?". Free Software Foundation (copy hosted by Chet Ramey, Case Western Reserve University).
quote: The name is an acronym for the 'Bourne-Again SHell', a pun on Stephen Bourne, the author of the direct ancestor of the current Unix shell sh
note: Same section: 'Bash is largely compatible with sh and incorporates useful features from the Korn shell ksh and the C shell csh.' gnu.org refused automated fetching, so the maintainer's mirror was used.

label: shell scripting style
citation: Wall, L. (1987). perl(1) manual page, Perl 1.0 (header dated 87/12/18). Distributed with Perl 1.0 (2.11BSD source archive).
quote: It combines (in the author's opinion, anyway) some of the best features of C, sed, awk, and sh, so people familiar with those languages should have little difficulty with it.
note: In 1987 'sh' meant the Bourne shell; the same page adds 'Language historians will also note some vestiges of csh, Pascal, and even BASIC-PLUS.' The current perl(1) at perldoc.perl.org says 'sed, awk, and sh' and drops C.

label: text patterns
citation: Wall, L. (1987). perl(1) manual page, Perl 1.0 (header dated 87/12/18). Distributed with Perl 1.0 (2.11BSD source archive).
quote: Perl is a interpreted language optimized for scanning arbitrary text files, extracting information from those text files, and printing reports based on that information.
note: Same DESCRIPTION: Perl 'combines ... some of the best features of C, sed, awk, and sh' and 'There are also translators to turn your sed and awk scripts into perl scripts.' The page names awk as a source but does not single out its patterns; the regex side is equally credited to sed.
suggested_label: awk-style text scanning and report generation

label: C-like syntax
citation: Wall, L. (1987). perl(1) manual page, Perl 1.0 (header dated 87/12/18). Distributed with Perl 1.0 (2.11BSD source archive).
quote: Expression syntax corresponds quite closely to C expression syntax.
note: The same page lists C first among 'the best features of C, sed, awk, and sh'.

label: C-like syntax
citation: Aho, A. V., Kernighan, B. W. & Weinberger, P. J. (1979). Awk — A Pattern Scanning and Processing Language. Software: Practice and Experience 9(4) (copy hosted at awk.dev).
quote: The for statement is also exactly that of C
note: The paper also says 'the C increment ++ and decrement -- operators are also available' and that printf matches 'the standard I/O library used with the programming language C'. Venue taken from the file name and standard bibliographies; the PDF's first page shows only Bell Laboratories.

label: associative arrays
citation: Aho, A. V., Kernighan, B. W. & Weinberger, P. J. (1979). Awk — A Pattern Scanning and Processing Language. Software: Practice and Experience 9(4) (copy hosted at awk.dev).
quote: Non-numeric array subscripts give awk a capability rather like the associative memory of Snobol tables.
note: The designers compare the feature to SNOBOL tables but do not say they borrowed it. Aho's 2016 Simple Talk interview names grep as the main inspiration and does not mention SNOBOL.

label: string scanning, same designer (Griswold)
citation: Griswold, R. E. (1994). Icon in the Humanities. TEXT Technology 4(1), 13-19 (online version updated 1996, University of Arizona).
quote: The design of Icon was motivated by the desire to recast some features of SNOBOL4 in more general ways and to provide facilities that SNOBOL4 lacks.
note: Griswold also calls Icon 'in some ways, a successor to SNOBOL4' and says string scanning answered weaknesses in SNOBOL4's pattern matching. The Icon Version 5 Reference Manual (Griswold et al., 1981; https://gmorph.cs.arizona.edu/icon/ftp/doc/tr81_4a.pdf) says SNOBOL4-style patterns 'were replaced by the concept of string scanning'. String scanning is Icon's replacement for SNOBOL4 patterns, not something taken from SNOBOL.
suggested_label: SNOBOL4 pattern matching recast as string scanning

label: generators (yield)
citation: Schemenauer, N., Peters, T. & Hetland, M. L. (2001). PEP 255 – Simple Generators. Python Enhancement Proposals.
quote: generators in Icon, a novel language where every expression is a generator. There are differences among these, but the basic idea is the same
note: The Motivation section cites Icon together with Sather and CLU iterators as prior art, and the Q&A compares Python with Icon's 'return expr' semantics.

label: indentation, built-in types
citation: van Rossum, G. (2009). Early Language Design and Development. The History of Python (blog).
quote: Python's use of indentation comes directly from ABC ... Python's major data types also derive from ABC, though with some modifications.
note: The same post credits ABC with the colon before indented blocks and with tuple packing and unpacking. Guido's 1996 foreword to Programming Python says indentation 'derives directly from ABC'.

label: modules, exceptions, classes
citation: Kuchling, A. M. (1998). LJ Interviews Guido van Rossum. Linux Journal.
quote: the Modula-3 final report was being written there at about the same time. What I learned there showed up in Python's exception handling, modules, and the fact that methods explicitly contain "self" in their parameter list.
note: Guido credits his DEC SRC exposure to Modula-2+ and Modula-3. For classes, the Python Tutorial §9 says the class mechanism 'is a mixture of the class mechanisms found in C++ and Modula-3'.

label: class mechanism (with Modula-3)
citation: Python Software Foundation (current ed.). The Python Tutorial, §9 Classes. docs.python.org.
quote: Python's class mechanism adds classes with a minimum of new syntax and semantics. It is a mixture of the class mechanisms found in C++ and Modula-3.
note: The same section uses C++ terms (members 'public', member functions 'virtual') and credits the explicit self argument to Modula-3.

label: operators, expression syntax
citation: Kuchling, A. M. (1998). LJ Interviews Guido van Rossum. Linux Journal.
quote: C is a second influence, second only to ABC in importance. Most of Python's keywords, such as break, continue and others, are identical to C's, as are operator priorities.
note: Guido also says early extension modules such as socket and POSIX wrap the UNIX C functions. His 1996 foreword says he 'borrowed from C too, but only its least controversial features'.

label: list comprehensions
citation: Kuchling, A. M. & Zadka, M. (2000). What's New in Python 2.0, §List Comprehensions. Python documentation.
quote: The idea of list comprehensions originally comes from the functional programming language Haskell
note: Same paragraph: Greg Ewing wrote the first patch and Skip Montanaro kept it up to date. The PEP 202 text was not checked.

label: joins, group-by via pandas (library-mediated)
citation: McKinney, W. (2010). Data Structures for Statistical Computing in Python. Proceedings of the 9th Python in Science Conference (SciPy 2010).
quote: This is akin to a SQL join operation between two tables.
note: The paper also says 'This concept of "group by" is a built-in feature of many data-oriented languages, such as R and SQL.' The SQL influence reaches pandas, not the Python language itself.

label: data frames via pandas (library-mediated)
citation: McKinney, W. (2010). Data Structures for Statistical Computing in Python. Proceedings of the 9th Python in Science Conference (SciPy 2010).
quote: pandas provides a similarly-named DataFrame class which implements much of the functionality of its R counterpart, though with some important enhancements (namely, built-in data alignment)
note: The R influence reaches pandas, not the Python language itself.

label: C-like syntax, function names
citation: The PHP Group (current ed.). History of PHP. PHP Manual.
quote: The language was deliberately designed to resemble C in structure, making it an easy adoption for developers familiar with C, Perl, and similar languages.
note: On function names, Rasmus Lerdorf wrote on php-internals (2 Jan 2014, https://externals.io/message/70896) that 'The function names and argument order, for the most part, were taken directly from these underlying libraries', citing MySQL's C API.

label: syntax, $ variables
citation: The PHP Group (current ed.). History of PHP. PHP Manual.
quote: It had Perl-like variables, automatic interpretation of form variables, and HTML embedded syntax. The syntax itself was similar to that of Perl, albeit much more limited, simple, and somewhat inconsistent.
note: This describes PHP/FI (1995-96).

label: PHP plus gradual typing
citation: Verlaguet, J. & Menghrajani, A. (2014, March 20). Hack: a new programming language for HHVM. Engineering at Meta (Facebook Engineering blog).
quote: Hack has deep roots in PHP. In fact, most PHP files are already valid Hack files. ... Technically speaking, Hack is a 'gradually typed' language
note: This describes Hack at launch (2014); its later divergence from PHP was not checked. docs.hhvm.com returned no readable text.

label: blocks, everything is an object
citation: Ruby community (current ed.). About Ruby. ruby-lang.org (official site).
quote: Ruby follows the influence of the Smalltalk language by giving methods and instance variables to all of its types.
note: The 'everything is an object' part is stated as a Smalltalk influence. Blocks are only a resemblance: the official FAQ says 'Like Smalltalk, everything in Ruby is an object, and Ruby has blocks', but the About page says 'Blocks are inspired by functional languages' (Lisp), and a 2019 recap of a Matz talk credits blocks to CLU.
suggested_label: everything is an object (pure OO model)

label: iterators, yield
citation: AppFolio Engineering Blog (2019, July 3). Ruby's Roots and Matz's Leadership (recap of a Matz talk at Cookpad, Bristol).
quote: Matz feels that blocks are the greatest invention of Ruby (I agree.) He got the idea from a 1970s language called CLU from MIT, which called them "iterators"
note: This is a second-hand recap of Matz's talk. Matz's own ruby-list:102 post (30 Jan 1996, https://blade.ruby-lang.org/ruby-list/102) only says CLU also has iterators, not that Ruby took them from CLU. No primary attribution was found.

label: clean object model
citation: Ruby community (current ed.). About Ruby. ruby-lang.org (official site).
quote: Its creator, Yukihiro "Matz" Matsumoto, blended parts of his favorite languages (Perl, Smalltalk, Eiffel, Ada, and Lisp) to form a new language
note: The influence is documented but not 'clean object model'. The 2019 AppFolio recap of a Matz talk says begin/end keywords, if/elsif/else/end 'comb indentation' and rescue/ensure/retry came from Eiffel.

label: regex, scripting
citation: Matsumoto, Y. (1999, June 4). Post on Ruby's history. ruby-talk mailing list, message 382.
quote: I knew Perl (Perl4, not Perl5), but I didn't like it really, because it had smell of toy language ... Then, I reorganized the features in Perl into class library, and implemented them.
note: The official Ruby FAQ says 'Like Perl, Ruby is good at text processing'. Regex specifically is credited to Perl only by secondary sources, e.g. twobithistory.org (2017): 'Ruby borrows much of Perl's regular expression handling and standard library.'

label: syntax
citation: Valim, J. (2016, February 26). Re: Any Erlang Devs Contemplating Elixir? erlang-questions mailing list.
quote: Elixir is not Ruby (and it could never be in the Erlang VM). Elixir also isn't about Ruby syntax (the same way Erlang isn't about Prolog syntax)
note: Valim's analogy implies a surface-syntax lineage but plays it down. No explicit designer statement of borrowing was found. Wikipedia lists Ruby under 'Influenced by' without a citation, and Valim was a Rails core team member (Code BEAM 2014 bio).

label: processes, OTP, the BEAM
citation: Elixir team (current ed.). Introduction to Mix (Mix and OTP guide). Elixir official documentation, hexdocs.
quote: OTP (Open Telecom Platform) is a set of libraries that ships with Erlang. Erlang developers use OTP to build robust, fault-tolerant applications.
note: The guide says it will show 'how many aspects from OTP integrate with Elixir, including supervision trees'. The elixir-lang.org homepage says Elixir is 'running on the battle-tested Erlang VM'.
